### Time to make decisions on new mine 

### investment _page 2_ 

World consumption of primary copper is forecast to reach almost 40 million tonnes in 2030, resulting in a potential deficit of some 8.3 million tonnes of copper mine output as current mining operations fail to meet demand.  This gap will attract investment in new mine projects after the current economic downturn.  Decisions on investment need to be taken now.  Using CRU’s Compass Model and its production costs database, CRU has forecast long run marginal costs and long term copper prices to act as a guide in strategic decision making. 

### Strikes in Chile – Not always necessary, but part of the system _page 9_ 

Strikes are part of the collective labour contract negotiation process under Chilean law.  If no agreement is reached after a certain period, then a legal strike can begin.  In the latest round of negotiations, unionised employees at Escondida, agreed to a generous pay and benefits package – the largest in recent history – avoiding a strike, whilst at Spence a less generous offer was rejected and workers went on strike in early October.  State-owned Codelco cannot match the offers made by the private sector and must take a different approach.  High copper prices have raised workers expectations and their elevated wage demands, if met, will increase operating costs, whilst strikes will disrupt production.

# Time to make decisions on new mine investment 

#### Introduction 

The world has witnessed a quicker economic recovery than expected and the copper price has been supported by market sentiment in the past few months.  Copper prices are forecast to remain above US$6,000/t until 2012 when the market will move into deficit, generating another price hike.  The gap between future consumption of primary copper and potential mine production has expanded due to increasing demand from China and restrictions on mine projects in terms of resource, technology and finance.  This gap will attract investment in new mine projects after the economic downturn – decisions on investment need to be taken now. 

Despite the fall in investment costs in 2009, the conversion costs of mining, smelting and refining are expected to move upwards.  Miners face greater challenges in finding world class deposits in low risk (politically stable) regions, and both miners and smelters/refiners have faced rising energy prices since May 2009.  As a result, the long run marginal costs (LRMC) of copper will continue to rise.  CRU has used its **_Compass Model_** to analyse the LRMC of copper.  The model assumes that in the long term, prices trend towards the LRMC set by the supply fundamentals of the industry.  Based on CRU’s database of production costs in existing and anticipated operations, the **_Long Term Copper Outlook_** provides a fo

recast of the LRMC and the long term copper price, as well as a guide towards capturing the investment opportunities that are now emerging. 

#### Over the risks, preparing for the opportunities 

Over the last six months, the copper price has bounced back from its lowest point in early 2009 and now stands at around US$6,700/t.  Stockpiling in China, both by the government and by speculators, since Q1 2009, has supported the price.  Strong demand for refined copper in China and India continues to encourage smelting capacity expansions and the refined copper market will remain in surplus through to 2011 and will be in balance in 2012.  CRU forecasts, however, that the market balance will move into deficit from 2013 after the economy picks up. 

The current financial restrictions have hampered the development of new mine projects at a time when new mine supply will be required as soon as 2012.  The need to develop smaller projects is key, given that world class deposits are increasingly rare.  Opportunities exist and investment decisions need to be made now if new mine output will be sufficient to meet future demand. 

#### LRMC overview and the CRU Compass Model 

CRU takes the view that in the long run the dominating driver of the copper price is the LRMC of mining, smelting and refining, which indicate the cost of bringing incremental production to the market.  After analysing a group of projects serving as potential sources of new copper mine production in the coming decades, CRU believes that the development of African mines will be of critical importance in bridging the gap between existing supply and growing demand.  New African mines have competitive operating costs, good quality resources and most are open pit mines.  In terms of smelters and refineries, we believe the driver of LRMC will be new smelters and refiners in China as they play a crucial role in meeting Chinese and world demand for refined copper. 

CRU has used its Compass Model to track and analyse the LRMC of copper, in order to produce a set of guidelines for the long term copper price forecasts needed in strategic decision-making.  The basic approach of the Compass Model is to recognise that the dynamics of price setting in commodity markets are fundamentally different in the short term and in the long term.  In the short term, supply and demand decisions are somewhat independent of one another.  Given the capital-intensive nature of mining and

metallurgical operations and the related high level of quasi-fixed and fixed costs in the overall financial structure, supply decisions tend to be resource driven.  Demand decisions are a function of global economic activity.  In the long term, however, markets are self-correcting.  Periods of high prices encourage producers to invest in additional supply capacity and may discourage consumers from developing new applications

.  Periods of very low prices lead to a lack of investment in supply capacity and may eventually encourage additional consumption as well.  Therefore in the long term, prices trend towards an average level that is set by the supply fundamentals of the industry. 

In the long term, metal supply can be increased.  It has been argued that demand will create, at a price, its own supply.  Our forecasting procedure reflects this dynamic.  The Compass Model simulates prices returning from their level at the end of the short term forecasting period to the trend of LRMC over a transition period.  There are therefore two main forecasting issues in the long term structural model.  The first is to make a correct projection of LRMC.  The second is to simulate a reasonable transition process. 

The Compass Model identifies and forecasts the economics of marginal projects that are expected to influence the industry’s pricing dynamic in the long term.  Because there is some uncertainty over the identity of future long run marginal projects, we have examined a range of possible benchmark projects, calculated LRMC at each of them, and then selected those that appear to be most viable from an overall industry development perspective.  This process enables us to consider a variety of economic risks as well as the full range of structural risks such as new technologies and resource depletion. 

Prices are forecast separately for copper in concentrates and for the conversion of concentrates into copper metal.  The price of metal is the sum of these two components.  We have analysed historical data on prices and treatment charges for copper in order to develop historical data on the two components of the overall price. 

The first step in the price forecasting process is to project the price of copper in concentrates, which is driven by Short Run Marginal Costs (SRMC) and LRMC at the mining stage.  We have identified the balance of the copper market from our forecast of inventory levels in relation to consumption.  The next step is to price the conversion of copper from concentrate into metal.  This is driven by SRMC and LRMC at the smelting/refining stage.  The criteria used in this case are not copper inventories, but custom smelter operating rates.  The structure of the copper market means that most of the price risk is passed back to the miners.  Smelters are highly capital-intensive facilities and also have a high level of quasifixed operating costs in relation to truly variable costs.  Smelters therefore tend to bid treatment charges down in order to try to fill capacity when operating rates are low, and increase prices when operating rates are high.  Finally, we have added together the price of mining and the price of smelting in order to derive the overall price of copper metal, which can then be converted into real terms by applying the relevant US GDP deflator. 

#### Mine operating costs will increase from 2011 onwards 

Global copper consumption is expected

to reach almost 40 million tonnes in 2030, which will result in a gap of the order of 8.3 million tonnes in copper mine production by 2030. Current mine operations will not be able to meet the future demand. **Note:** The LRMC quoted in this article are based on CRU’s copper price forecasts as of September 2009. © 2009 CRU International Limited confidential www.crumonitor.com COPPER STUDIES November 2009 9 # Strikes in Chile – Not always necessary, but part of the system #### Introduction In H2 2009, the Chilean copper mining industry is facing industrial action related to the negotiation of collective labour agreements at many large mine operations. When a collective labour contract is abou

t to expire, company management and unionised workers begin negotiations over the conditions for the next collective contract.  If no agreement is reached prior to the end of the current contract, there is a voluntary mediation period after which the labour union is in a legal position to officially begin a strike. 

The collective negotiation legislation applies to every labour union across all industries in Chile. These negotiations assume more importance in the mining industry, however, because they involve larger amounts of money and have a greater impact on the local economy.  The collective negotiation process in Chile differs from that in other countries:  firstly, Chilean legislation establishes strikes as the next step in the process if an agreement has not been reached;  and secondly, these negotiation processes are undertaken every two to four years (collective contracts cannot last any longer). 

#### Legal structure and procedures for collective labour agreements 

The Chilean Legal Labour Code ( _Cуdigo del Trabajo_ ) was approved in July 2002, enacted in January 2003 and last updated in August 2009.  This Code sets out the rules and regulations for collective labour agreements, within which labour strikes are considered legal and follow strict procedures and deadlines. The Code regulates and controls all procedures and rights of employers and employees, including all labour union issues and procedures during a strike.  It is administrated by the Ministry of Labour, which is independent and separate from the Ministry of Mining. 

The Code applies to all industries but it is in the mining industry where labour unions are most demanding in the renewal of collective contracts, because they perceive mining companies have higher revenues in comparison to other industries.  They are also aware that strikes at copper mines have a greater impact on the Chilean economy than strikes in other industries.  A strike in 2006 undertaken by workers of an important Chilean retail company with a presence in other South American countries, for example, involved an initial offer of a US$350 bonus, whilst workers demanded a US$600 bonus.  In comparison, unionised workers at Escondida managed to obtain a US$16,750 bonus. 

The average collective negotiation process takes as long as 85 days (including a one-month strike); but there is no time limit for the negotiation period as a strike can last longer than a month.  During the negotiation process operations are unlikely to run at normal levels of productivity. 

The most relevant points of the legal framework concerning collective labour contracts or agreements in the mining industry are as follows: 

- Official negotiations between management and unionised workers start 45 days before the previous contract expires.  These negotiations can begin before this official time frame if company management wants to propose an early offer and try to avoid official negotiations. If no agreement is reached between

the management and the labour union by the time the current contract expires, a five-day government mediation period can start if agreed by both parties. This mediation period can be extended for a further five-day period if both parties agree. Finally, if there is no agreement after the total five- or ten-day mediation period, a legal strike begins. Is important to note that the government mediation is represented by the labour, not the mining, authorities. © 2009 CRU International Limited confidential www.crumonitor.com COPPER STUDIES November 2009 10 - Company management can hire temporary workers during the strike period. If the latest offer to renew the collective agreement includes a pay rise at least equivalent to the rate of inflation, temporary workers can be hired as soon as the strike begins. Otherwise, temporary workers can be hired 15 days after the beginning of the strike. - Every employee must be free to choose whether to join a labour union or not. The company cannot differentiate between non-unionised workers and unionised workers. At the same time, the labour union cannot take any measures to persuade workers to join the union. - The company does not have any obligation to pay salaries to unionised workers on strike, and unionised workers on strike do not have the right to ask for payment of their salaries. - 15 days after management can hire temporary workers, workers on strike can individually return to work. They would receive at least the same benefits that were contained in the latest offer. - If at any moment during the strike more than half the unionised workers have individually returned to work, the strike will officially end on that day. In this case, the rest of the workers on strike must return to work under the conditions laid out in the latest offer. #### Typical collective labour agreements Collective la

bour agreements typically comprise a percentage wage increase above the rate of inflation and a one-off bonus linked to the end of the negotiation, usually called an end-of-conflict bonus.  Other benefits include health and education benefits for workers’ families and in most cases, company managers in the mining industry agree to lend a certain sum of money as a low-interest ‘soft’ loan to each worker. 

Collective labour agreements have to last between two and four years by law.  Companies tend to aim to settle longer agreements, in order to delay the next negotiation process and to enable them to make better forecasts of labour costs.  On the other hand, labour unions aim for agreement periods as short as possible, to shorten the period before they have an opportunity to ask for a wage increase and the end-ofconflict bonus.

<u>www.crumonitor.com</u> COPPER STUDIES November 2009

Although the collective agreement is a contract between the employer and unionised employees, nonunionised workers will usually also receive the benefits.  The main reason behind this is the management’s aim to keep as many workers as possible out of the labour union, without offering any direct incentive.  This practice is not mandatory for the company management;  it is just a way of trying not to increase the share of unionised workers in the company. 

In terms of assessing the costs of these collective agreements, in some cases bonuses can be considered as a redistribution of profits, and not an increase in costs.  On the other hand, wage rises must be considered as an increase in costs. 

###### Advisors helping labour unions 

As collective negotiation processes in Chile occur periodically and, in the case of the copper industry, involve high levels of resources and money, advisors and consultancy companies specialising in this area have been established. 

As of September 2009, the employed labour force in Chile totalled 6,537,583 people according to the National Statistics Institute ( _Instituto Nacional de Estadisticas_ , INE).  Approximately 5,557,000 were entitled to belong to a labour union;  the rest were unable to join a labour union because of legal restrictions related to the number of internal employees or the type of company for which they work.  Of those workers entitled to join a union, only 13% are effectively listed in one of the 9,300 labour unions in the country.  In the case of the mining industry, that share rises to 90%.  This figure compares with OECD member countries where 30% of workers are unionised.  Of the total of 722,000 workers listed in a labour union across Chile, we estimate that around 2% work in the mining industry. 

In 2006, the collective negotiation process at Escondida (operated by BHP Billiton) involved a 25-day strike, and the labour union hired a firm of advisors which was specifically formed to assist in that negotiation.  This firm, composed of 19 professionals i

ncluding engineers, economists and lawyers, earned US$535,000 for that work. 

The next collective negotiation process undertaken at Escondida this year was different.  A generous early offer made by BHP Billiton was accepted by the labour union, thus avoiding a complicated situation as negotiations were due to start in early December which would have overlapped with the last week of political campaigning for the Chilean presidential elections.  The labour union was assisted by a firm of six professionals which won the bidding process held in September 2008.  This firm has considerable expertise in labour issues.  It has assisted every labour union in the largest division of Codelco – the world’s largest copper company – for more than ten years.  During this year’s negotiations at Escondida, the firm held frequent meetings with the company’s authorities.  The process resulted in the most generous offer to workers ever seen in Chile and avoided official negotiations between managers and workers during December.  The firm of advisors earned US$205,000, less than the sum earned in the 2006 negotiation process. 

In general, the most recognised advisors in this field can earn up to US$75 per unionised worker, whatever the outcome of negotiations.  Other advisors could earn higher amounts per unionised worker, but that would be dependent on the benefits agreed for the workers.  As there could be around 560 unionised workers at Spence or around 6,000 at Codelco Norte, it is clear that this activity can be highly lucrative. 

These labour advisors assist labour unions not only in the mining industry, but in every industry, in collective negotiation procedures as well as in other matters.  Due to the high levels of trust needed between workers and advisors in this kind of service, there are few (less than 20) advisors who hold a large share of the market and who are the most well-known advisors. 

Advisors have different styles of working and negotiating with companies.  Some look for confrontation and create a tense relationship with company managers, often demanding too much for the workers.  Other advisors have a different reputation and resolve differences between managers and

workers, aligning workers’ demands with the company’s ability to offer.  The style and reputation of every advisor is well known by union leaders, especially in the mining industry;  whatever type of negotiation the union leaders are looking for, the union will easily know who to hire. 

#### Latest collective labour negotiations in Chile 

Probably the most significant event regarding strikes in the Chilean copper industry occurred in Q3 2006, when unionised workers at Escondida (as mentioned above) held a 25-day strike before agreeing a collective labour contract with the company.  This strike was the longest and most harmful – in terms of production losses – for th

e industry in recent Chilean history.  In addition, the final collective labour agreement was highly beneficial for the workers, who managed to obtain a US$16,750 bonus and a 5% wage increase for the next 40 months.  This agreement made workers at Escondida the best paid copper mine workers in South America.  Their initial demands had been even higher, comprising an end-ofconflict bonus close to US$30,000 and a 13% wage increase. 

This agreement set a precedent for collective negotiations in Chile and marked the beginning of a period of harder negotiations between managers and mine labour unions.  For example, at the end of 2006 state-owned Codelco experienced no strikes within its mine operations; but the end-of-conflict bonuses paid were considerably higher than those paid in the company’s previous collective agreements.  Codelco Norte’s workers received a US$15,000 bonus in 2006 compared with a US$6,600 bonus in 2003 (see the table on the following page). 

The situation has not changed much since then.  A couple of important collective negotiations have been concluded so far through H2 2009 and others are still to be resolved this year.  One of the important negotiations to have taken place this year concerns Escondida, where a complicated situation was expected as negotiations were due to start just a week before the presidential elections.  An early offer to renew the collective labour agreement made by the managers was approved by 72% of unionised workers, however.  As stated above, the offer at Escondida is the most generous ever seen in Chile and consisted of an end-of-conflict bonus of around US$25,750 per worker (the highest in recent history), a one-off 5% wage increase, a 44-month contract duration, social benefits for families and access to a US$6,300 loan at highly favourable terms.  To put in context, the US$25,750 bonus is roughly between two and three times Chile’s per capita GDP and considerably higher than the annual wage of an average worker in any other industry in Chile. 

#### Spence – the longest negotiation process 

After several strike threats by mine workers and frustrated negotiations between mine management and the labour union, in October 2009 unionised workers at BHP Billiton’s Spence mine began a strike.  This mine started-up in 2006 and the first collective labour agreement expired in September 2009.  Unionised workers at Spence rejected three different offers made by the company management.  The last of these consisted of a US$19,250 bonus, a 4% wage increase and a 36-month contract duration.  The workers’ demands consisted of a 5.5% wage increase, a 24-month contract duration and a US$27,500 bonus (US$13,750 a year).  This is more ambitious than the deal recently reached at Escondida and higher than the latest agreements made at other copper mines in Chile (see the following table). 

After rejecting the final offer made by company management before the current contract expired, and after the unsuccessful ten

-day voluntary mediation period, unionised workers at Spence started a legal strike on October 13th , 2009. As of mid-November, there had been few approaches to resume negotiations during the strike. The company’s first approach to negotiate came only after 10 days after the strike had begun; it requested absolute secure conditions and asked workers to leave the camp they were using in the surrounding area. The SXEW plant is still in operation and leaching at the minimum level to keep it operating. To fully stop the plant would involve higher costs. A few non-unionised employees are working at the operation. The Spence management could have replaced workers on strike since the strike started, but they decided not to replace them at that time. The probable reason behind this decision was that managers wanted to let unionised workers know that the company did not urgently need to resume production, even though the union leaders claim that the company is losing US$3M a day due to the strike. Nevertheless, after more than 20 days of the strike, job advertisements for mine operator replacements at Spence appeared in the newspapers. ###### Legal issues involved A few days before the current collective contract expired at Spence, union leaders decided to penalise each unionised employee who individually returned to work during a potential strike. The penalty was a US$13,250 bill of exchange. This practice could be considered illegal as Chilean law considers it disloyal conduct towards the unionised worker, given that every worker should be free to choose whether to belong to a labour union. In response, and after several days of the strike and to protect workers’ rights, the Spence management offered legal assistance to each unionised worker interested in returning to work, in order to avoid the fine and costs to be covered by the employee. The US$13,250 bills of exchange may not now be charged, as company management officially reported this potentially illegal practice to the Chilean Labour Court a week after the strike began. © 2009 CRU International Limited confidential www.crumonitor.com COPPER STUDIES November 2009 14 ###### An end to the strike looks likely In the latest developments, some striking workers invaded the Spence mine site during the week ending November 20th and allegedly sabotaged equipment and seized pumps that circulate sulphuric acid used for the leaching of ore. Subsequently, BHP shut down the Spence mine. At the time of going to print, an end to the strike at Spence now looks likely. On Monday November 23rd , workers at Spence voted to end the 42-day strike, after agreeing a new wage deal with owner BHP. The deal came after a leading Chilean mine union last week threatened to halt output at other mines owned by BHP Billiton in solidarity with the Spence strikers. Once workers have signed their new contracts they are expected to return to work on either Wednesday November 25th of Thursday November 26th . The deal includes a 4% pay rise for union workers during the duration of the 41-month contract, as well as other bonuses and benefits. The agreed pay increase is lower than the union’s original demand of 5.5%

, but equals the company’s last offer.  The duration of the contract, however, is longer than both the union’s demand of 24 months and the company’s last offer of 36 months. 

#### Next collective negotiations in the industry 

In addition to Escondida and Spence, some other important copper operations still have to negotiate the renewal of their collective labour agreements in 2009.  Two of these operations are Andina and Codelco Norte, two of the five divisions of the state-owned Codelco, whose collective contracts expire at the end of November and December 2009, respectively. 

Although the next collective negotiations for these two Codelco divisions may take the historical agreement at Escondida as a precedent, the fact that the latter relates to a private company marks an important difference to the Andina and Codelco Norte operations.  The different productivity levels seen at Codelco’s operations and private operations in general are a clear restriction for Codelco to reach the same levels of benefits.  The current Codelco administration – associated with Michelle Bachelet’s government – has never suffered a strike by internal workers within its operations, however.  It has achieved this by offering high bonuses but low wage increases, thereby maintaining costs under a certain level and redistributing profits linked to high copper prices.  Nevertheless, the bonuses offered by Escondida are too high for any of Codelco’s operations. 

Currently, Andina’s labour unions are officially negotiating with management after rejecting an early offer made by the management in order to avoid collective negotiations.  On November 21<sup>st</sup> , workers at Andina approved a new labour contract on offer from Codelco.  The deal includes a single 3.0% wage increase, about US$15,000 in bonuses and benefits per worker and US$5,000 in soft loans.  The new 36month contract will commence on December 1<sup>st</sup> , 2009. 

Codelco Norte’s management decided not to bring forward negotiations by means of an early offer to the labour unions, and will carry out the negotiations under the regulated time frames.  The three Codelco Norte labour unions which have to negotiate their respective collective contracts in December have let it be known they will negotiate together, which means that all 6,500 employees included in the three unions will demand the same conditions.  Union leaders have agreed not to ask for an end-of-conflict bonus, arguing that this bonus distorts the collective negotiation process and creates false hopes in workers’ expectations.  Instead, the labour union will ask for health, education and housing benefits equivalent to US$21,000 together with a 7.5% wage increase. 

On November 20<sup>th</sup> , workers at BHP Billiton’s Cerro Colorado mine accepted a contract deal which includes around US$20,000 in bonuses per worker and a single 4.8% pay rise for the duration of the 41month contract.  The current contract expires on January 31<sup>st</su

p> , 2010 and the early settlement will avert the possibility of any strike action. These strikes follow procedures which are strictly laid out in the Labour Code and are under the supervision of the labour authorities. If no agreement is reached after a certain period, then a legal strike has to begin. The company must recognise this strike procedure as part of employees’ rights. Not every employee of every Chilean company is able to form a labour union, however, as there are some restrictions linked to the amount of workers in the respective companies. On the one hand, Chilean law establishes strikes as a way for employees to put pressure on companies which do not accept their demands. On the other hand, the same Chilean law gives companies methods of sustaining operations while their workers are on strike; and there are no set levels relating to the share of revenues which must be passed on to workers. |Collective labour contract expiry dates in Chile's copper industry| |---| ||||**2009 forecast production**
